results.claim: Planar two-exit instances admit a cyclic two-gate decomposition. Let the exits be p,q and let B=N(p)∩N(q). Every component of G−({p,q}∪B) is adjacent to at most two vertices of B; when |B|≥3, those two are consecutive in the cyclic order of B around the exits.
results.proof_sketch: The edges from {p,q} to B form K_{2,|B|}. For |B|≥3 this embedded skeleton is 2-connected. Euler's formula gives |B| faces; simplicity and bipartiteness make every facial boundary have length at least four, while the total facial-boundary length is 2|E|=4|B|. Thus every face is a 4-cycle p-b_i-q-b_{i+1}-p. A connected component disjoint from the skeleton lies in one face, so its B-neighbors are among that face's two consecutive gates. For |B|≤2 the assertion is immediate.

results.claim: There is a linear-time classification when the exits have the same independent neighborhood. After deleting a possible irrelevant edge pq, suppose N(p)=N(q)=B and B is independent. The fugitive wins exactly when (i) s∈{p,q}∪B, (ii) s has a neighbor in B, or (iii) s has a neighbor w having two distinct neighbors in B.
results.proof_sketch:
The three conditions give explicit wins. In (ii), move directly to an untouched b∈B; after Nemesis deletes one of bp,bq, use the other. In (iii), move to w. The three-edge sets {wb_i,b_ip,b_iq} for two gates b_1,b_2 are edge-disjoint, so one deletion spoils at most one; move to the other gate and escape.

Conversely, assume none holds. After the fugitive's first move to w, let C be its component outside {p,q}∪B. The decomposition gives C at most two boundary gates, and w is adjacent to at most one. Nemesis prepares that gate by deleting one exit edge, or prepares an arbitrary boundary gate if w sees none. Before the other gate can be entered, Nemesis gets another deletion with which to prepare it. Whenever a prepared gate is entered, she deletes its other exit edge. Since B is independent, leaving that dead gate enters an outside component in which it is one of at most two boundary gates, leaving at most one new gate to prepare. Induction prevents entry into any unprepared gate. Finite edge deletion forces termination without escape. The B=∅ case is immediate, and the conditions are testable by adjacency scans.

results.claim: Two broader target-relevant subclasses are linearly solvable: (a) the graph induced by regular vertices is a forest, with arbitrary degrees; or (b) every regular vertex has degree at most three, with arbitrary exit degrees.
results.proof_sketch: Handle a start at an exit immediately and discard any exit-exit edge, which is irrelevant. Replace every regular-to-exit incidence vx by an edge from v to its own fresh degree-one exit leaf x_{v,x}, then remove the original exits. Regular positions and relevant deletable edges correspond bijectively, and a regular vertex is connected to an original exit exactly when it is connected to a corresponding leaf. Thus every play and outcome is preserved. In case (a), each transformed component containing a possible start is a tree. In case (b), the transformed graph has maximum degree at most three. The source's linear-time algorithms for trees and maximum-degree-three simple graphs apply, and the transformation has linear size.

results.claim: Internal-edge deletions are essential even for planar simple graphs with exactly two exits: constraining Nemesis to delete only exit-incident edges can change the winner. Let the exits be p,q, the start be s, and the other vertices be x,a,b, with edges pa,pb,qa,qb,ax,xs,ab. Nemesis wins the original game, but the Fugitive wins under that restriction.
results.proof_sketch:
The graph is simple and has the crossing-free straight-line drawing a=(0,0), b=(2,0), p=(1,1), q=(1,−1), x=(−1,0), s=(−2,0). In the original game, the only first move is s→x; Nemesis deletes xa, immediately leaving x in the exit-free component {s,x}.

Now restrict Nemesis to exit-incident deletions. After s→x her deletion touches a or b. If it touches b, then a is fresh; the Fugitive moves x→a, and the next deletion leaves an a-exit edge for an immediate win. If the first deletion touches a, move x→a. Nemesis must either leave a's remaining exit edge, which is used immediately, or delete it; in the latter case both b-exit edges and ab remain, so a→b reaches a fresh gate and one subsequent deletion cannot block both exits. These cases exhaust every permitted deletion.

results.claim: Nemesis is not invariant under edge subdivision, even on planar simple trees with exactly two exits. With exits p,q, start s, and regular vertex a, the graph with edges sa,ap,aq is a Fugitive win, while subdividing sa once with a new regular vertex x makes it a Nemesis win. More generally, replacing r parallel sa edges by the r paths s-x_i-a fails to preserve the winner for every r≥1.
results.proof_sketch: In the original multigraph M_r, the Fugitive moves directly s→a. One deletion cannot remove both ap and aq, so he exits next round. In the subdivided graph S_r, Nemesis maintains that no edge x_i-a survives after the Fugitive enters x_i: if he moves s→x_i while x_i-a is present, delete it; after a move into a previously cut branch or back to s, delete any remaining x_j-a. The Fugitive never reaches a, and after at most r such deletions his component has no exit. The graph S_r is simple and planar: draw r noncrossing parallel s-a arcs, subdivide each once, and attach p,q as leaves at a. For r=1, M_1 and S_1 are exactly the two simple planar trees in the claim. Thus neither subdivision nor the usual parallel-edge-to-path-bundle replacement preserves the outcome.

results.claim: The binary-escape-tree condition is not necessary even for planar simple graphs with exactly two exits. A seven-vertex counterexample has exits p,q, start s, regular vertices a,b,c,z, and edges pa,pb,qa,qb,ab,az,bz,bc,cz,cs.
results.proof_sketch:
An exact straight-line drawing is a=(0,0), b=(120,0), p=(60,80), q=(60,-80), z=(60,40), c=(90,10), s=(80,23); integer orientation tests show that no nonincident edges cross.

The fugitive moves s→c. If Nemesis deletes bc, move c→z. Her next deletion can spoil at most one of the edge-disjoint configurations {za,ap,aq} and {zb,bp,bq}; use the other common neighbor and then its surviving exit edge. If the first deletion is not bc, move c→b. Use bp or bq if either survives. If both have been deleted, they are exactly Nemesis's first two deletions, so ab,ap,aq remain; move b→a and then use whichever exit edge survives.

After exit splitting, only s and c can be roots within distance one of s. Vertex s has degree one. At root c, a regular leaf s is forbidden, so the two children must be b and z. Then z, a nonroot regular vertex, would need both a and the already-used b as children in addition to parent c, contradicting the tree condition. Hence no binary escape tree exists.

results.claim: The seven-vertex binary-escape-tree counterexample is vertex-minimal: no planar simple Nemesis instance with exactly two exits and at most six vertices has a Fugitive-winning regular start that fails the binary-escape-tree condition after the source's exit splitting and pruning.
results.proof_sketch: Relabeling fixes the exits as 0,1. An exact enumeration considered every edge subset for n=3,4,5,6. By Kuratowski's theorem, on at most six vertices planarity is decided by testing for the only possible subdivisions of K_5 or K_{3,3}: K_5, K_5 with one edge subdivided, and K_{3,3}. This retained 33,166 labeled planar graphs and 125,655 exit-connected regular starts. The deleted-edge recurrence and a separately phased evaluator agreed; 111,587 starts were Fugitive wins. For each, the check split every regular-exit incidence into a pendant exit, discarded exit-exit edges, iteratively pruned degree-one or degree-two regular vertices other than s, and kept the s-component. It then enumerated every transformed edge subset and every eligible root, accepting exactly connected acyclic subgraphs with root degree two, nonroot regular degree three, and exit leaves degree one, including a singleton exit root. Every winning start passed. The seven-vertex witness was a negative control and failed the condition, establishing the lower bound.

results.claim: An exact recurrence gives PSPACE membership and an O*(8^n) planar algorithm, although not a polynomial classification. For deleted-edge set D and current regular vertex v, W(D,v) holds iff some surviving move vw reaches an exit or, for every surviving edge e Nemesis might delete, w remains connected to an exit and W(D∪{e},w) holds.
results.proof_sketch: Precisely, W(D,v)=∃vw∉D [w is an exit ∨ ∀e∉D (w is connected to an exit in G−(D∪{e}) and W(D∪{e},w))]. The existential chooses the fugitive's move and the universal quantifies over Nemesis's possible deletion after that move; the connectivity conjunct implements immediate loss. Every recursive call strictly enlarges D, so evaluation is acyclic. There are at most n·2^m states with polynomial transition work. Depth-first evaluation has depth at most m and polynomial-size frames, proving PSPACE membership. For a simple planar graph with n≥3, m≤3n−6, so memoized evaluation takes O*(2^m)=O*(8^n); smaller instances are constant-size.

final_writeup:
This is a partial resolution. I did not obtain either a polynomial-time algorithm for all planar simple two-exit instances or a complete hardness reduction.

The main structural leverage is that the common neighbors of the two exits form a planar K_{2,k} skeleton. Its faces arrange those gates cyclically, and every remaining connected piece can touch at most two consecutive gates. Using this, the game is completely classified in linear time when both exits have the same neighborhood and that neighborhood is independent: the only winning configurations are an immediate gate, a gate one move away, or a first move exposing two gates simultaneously. Nemesis otherwise prepares and then kills boundary gates while following the fugitive from face to face.

Exit splitting also yields two substantial linear-time cases: arbitrary-degree instances whose regular core is a forest, and instances in which only the exits may have degree above three.

The seven-vertex construction shows why these results do not immediately extend to all planar two-exit graphs. A single edge between common-neighbor gates, combined with a small planar backup cycle, lets the fugitive win even though the paper's binary-escape-tree condition fails. Thus a general algorithm must account for tempo gained by moving through partially damaged gates; static escape-tree detection alone cannot classify the target. An exact exhaustive boundary check shows that seven vertices are necessary: every planar simple two-exit instance on at most six vertices that is a Fugitive win satisfies the tree condition after exit splitting and pruning.

A direct attempt to simplify the game by allowing Nemesis to delete only exit-incident edges also fails. In the six-vertex planar witness above, deleting the internal edge xa after the forced move s→x traps the Fugitive immediately. Without that internal deletion, the Fugitive can force passage through a and then, if necessary, the fresh adjacent gate b. Hence a general algorithm must track internal cuts as well as damage to exit gates.

Subdivision gives a separate obstruction to importing the planar-multigraph hardness proof. In the simple tree with edges sa,ap,aq, the Fugitive reaches a and then one of the two exits. Subdividing sa once lets Nemesis delete the new forward edge immediately after s→x and trap the Fugitive. More generally, replacing any number of parallel sa edges by internally disjoint two-edge paths has the same failure. Consequently, parallel edges cannot simply be eliminated by planar subdivision gadgets; any hardness transfer must compensate for the extra move-and-delete tempo.

The remaining unresolved core consists of the cyclic gate skeleton with edges or more general short connections between consecutive gates and arbitrary planar two-boundary pieces between them. The exact recurrence supplies a rigorous exponential baseline and PSPACE upper bound, but no matching lower bound is established here.
